Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.explanation: The Threat items describe a chronic interpersonal/home-intrusion danger template (monitoring for someone entering the home, planning escape routes, feeling unsafe specifically at night), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item about listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal/intrusion danger theme that is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma type of natural disaster. For a natural-disaster profile, loud sounds and generalized hypervigilance are plausible, but specifically monitoring for a person entering the home suggests a different trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: The appraisal that institutions failed to protect him is possible after a disaster, but in combination with the home-intrusion threat cue it contributes to a mixed interpersonal-threat profile rather than a coherent natural-disaster formulation. The rest of the profile centers on terror, overwhelm, and disorganized memory, so this item is questionable mainly because it pulls toward a different trauma narrative when paired with the flagged threat item.

vignette: At forty-five, David Vance lived alone in a quiet second-floor apartment, widowed and carrying the weight of a storm that had fractured his deployment in coastal Alabama seven years ago. He had been securing a field triage tent when the wind shifted, carrying a sound like a freight train derailing inside the canvas walls. The perimeter fencing sheared off, and the water came not as a wave but as a sudden, heavy wall that pinned his boots to the mud. He knew he had to move toward the screaming, but the sequence of it all-the snapping trees, the radio static, the way the ground itself seemed to tilt-refused to settle into a line. When he closed his eyes now, the terror hit him with the same force, a drowning pressure in his chest that made his hands shake so violently he had to step away from the sink and press his palms to his face until the flood of emotion receded. He learned to stop when the memories began, cutting himself off before the overwhelm could take hold, yet the event refused to arrange itself into a coherent story. He could never place who was treated first, only that everything had happened at once. The years that followed settled into a rhythm of quiet tension. David kept his military medic uniform pressed in his closet but found himself unable to move through the civilian VA clinic where he now worked as a trauma coordinator without his shoulders permanently forward. He was constantly on guard, his eyes tracking every doorway, every shift in floor traffic. A dropped clipboard or a slammed office door sent his heart hammering against his ribs, and he would freeze until the sound registered as harmless. Even on his days off, when he locked his apartment door and turned off the television, the stillness offered no relief. He paced the living room at night, his body remaining wired to guard against a threat that refused to appear, leaving him unable to let his shoulders drop even when he knew he was in a safe place. His work environment, once a place of purpose, now felt like a minefield of reminders. During morning rounds, the hiss of an autoclave or the sudden crackle of the overhead paging system would make his breath catch, and he would find himself stepping back from the supply cabinet, unable to trust the machinery he had once calibrated with his bare hands. He had come to believe that the rules he once trusted about how the world works had been completely shattered, that cause and effect no longer held any weight. He looked at his own reflection in the clinic's breakroom window and barely recognized the man staring back. The hands that had held pressure dressings and written triage tags now felt like strangers' tools. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; without the rhythm of duty, the days blurred into a hollow routine, and he felt like he did not know himself anymore. What finally brought him to this intake room was the sheer exhaustion of holding himself together. He had stopped attending the memorial gatherings, cancelled his evening walks when the weather turned sharp, and quietly stepped back from volunteer search committees rather than face the unpredictable demands of disaster drills. He sat now on the edge of the cushioned chair, fingers interlaced, waiting for the clinician to speak. He hoped, perhaps, that someone might help him untangle the knot in his chest, not because he expected a return to the man he used to be, but because the constant vigilance was finally leaving him too tired to stand. He was most afraid of losing control again, of being caught flat-footed when the next loud noise shattered his composure. He did not ask for the past to be undone; he only wanted to know how to live in a present that felt so fragile.
